title: Damodara, tied by love
hookLine: Yashoda chases her son with a stick, and every rope she ties comes up two fingers short
carry: love is the only rope that holds God

cards: The servants are busy elsewhere, and Yashoda is churning curd herself, pulling the rope back and forth around the churning stick, her bangles moving, singing, the text says, about the things her little boy has done.
Then the little boy arrives. He's hungry, he wants his mother, and he takes hold of the churning stick so she can't go on. She lifts him into her lap and feeds him.
A perfectly quiet scene. It's about to fall apart.

teach.b: On the fire, the milk starts to boil over. Yashoda sets Krishna down mid-meal and runs to it. He's furious.
He bites his lip, cracks open the pot of curd with a stone, slips into another room and eats butter in secret.

teach.h: A BROKEN POT, A MONKEY, A STICK.
teach.b: Yashoda comes back to a broken pot and no child. She finds him on an upturned mortar, handing butter from the hanging pot to a monkey. She picks up a stick.
He jumps down and runs, and she runs after him. The Bhagavata pauses to marvel: the one the yogis can't reach even with their minds is being chased around the yard by his mother. She catches him.
He cries and rubs his eyes. She drops the stick and decides to tie him to the mortar instead. The rope is too short, by two fingers' width.
She adds another. Still two fingers short.

Every rope in the house, always two fingers short, and the neighbor women laugh, and so does she. She's sweating now. Krishna sees how tired his mother is, and then, the text says, he lets himself be tied.
The Bhagavata says this is what the scene shows: the Lord lets himself be held by those who love him. That's the heart of bhakti, devotion. Not power, not cleverness, not even the yogis' meditation.
Nothing in the universe can hold him; a tired mother's love can, because he allows it. Tradition says this is where one of his names comes from: Damodara, the one with a rope around his waist.

how: Krishna bound by Yashoda's rope is remembered in his name Damodara, and some Vaishnava communities honor this story in the autumn month of Kartika with songs and lamps offered to Damodara.

o: the churning stick Yashoda uses to make butter
the heavy wooden mortar Krishna is tied to in the yard
a name of Krishna: the one with a rope at his waist

games.q: the churning morning — tap the pairs.
p: the love God lets hold him

s: Yashoda beats Krishna with the stick
she drops the stick when he cries, and decides to tie him instead.
the rope is too short no matter how much she adds
every rope in the house, and still two fingers short.
Krishna is finally tied because Yashoda is stronger
he sees how tired she is and lets himself be tied.

games.q: you're Yashoda. every rope in the house is two fingers short. what finally ties him?
o: a longer rope from the neighbors.
nothing, until he sees how hard you're trying and lets your love hold him.
Nanda, who comes home and holds him down.
games.why: seeing her effort, he lets himself be tied: the Bhagavata's picture of the Lord held by those who love him.

practice: People who love Damodara often light a small lamp before his image and sing to him. If you have a lamp or candle, light it; if not, picture one.
Bring to mind someone who has tried very hard for you, a parent, a grandparent, a teacher, and see them in the middle of that effort, a little tired. Say Damodara once, quietly.
If you don't pray, simply thank that person in your heart.

wordCard.voice: Damodara. The name tradition gives Krishna for the rope at his waist, after he let his tired mother finally tie him.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Damodara, a name of Krishna that tradition links to the rope at his waist.

carryVoice: Your line: love is the only rope that holds God. Tomorrow, two trees in the yard. Day eight hundred eighty-eight, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.9, Yashoda churning, the broken curd pot, the chase, the binding to the mortar, and the narrator's remark that the Lord is held by those devoted to him
